strengths: The paper provides a clean and useful theoretical characterization of why popular test-time guidance schemes (DPS posterior-mean, ΠGDM/LGD Gaussian, NDTM optimization) fail to sample the true Bayesian posterior. Theorems 4.1–4.3 formalize that these estimators are biased regardless of compute, which is a valuable clarification for the field.

The proposed CBG estimators (Eq. 16 reparameterization; Eq. 20 REINFORCE/self-normalized) are correctly derived and are genuinely consistent: the numerator/denominator limits recover the exact diffused likelihood gradient as K grows. The gradient-free variant also accommodates non-differentiable rewards, which is practically useful.

The Bayesian inference benchmark (SBI tasks with analytic priors and closed-form diffusion posteriors) is a well-controlled setting, and Figure 3/Table 1 convincingly show that CBG improves C2ST with more compute while the baselines plateau at biased distributions. Comparison against both likelihood-based and likelihood-free baselines is thorough.

Reproducibility is reasonably addressed: appendices give the exact tasks, priors, diffusion posteriors, hyperparameter sweeps, and chosen values, and the black-hole protocol follows InverseBench for fair comparison.
The paper is generally well written and the calibration framing is conceptually clear, with informative figures (Fig. 1, 2) illustrating the source of bias.
weaknesses: Originality is limited: the gradient-free estimator (Eq. 20) is essentially self-normalized importance sampling / SMC-style posterior-score estimation, which is very close to existing twisted-SMC diffusion guidance (e.g., Wu et al., 'Practical and Asymptotically Exact Conditional Sampling in Diffusion Models' / twisted diffusion sampler). These works are neither cited nor compared, and the concurrent work (Potaptchik et al., 2026) reportedly uses the same estimators, further reducing novelty.

Practical significance is undermined by cost and marginal gains. The black-hole experiment requires ~2h40 per image on an H100 with K=512, M=50, yet only marginally beats PnP-DM (26.10 vs 26.07 PSNR) and DPS (25.86). The O(NM) nested-sampling cost is a serious limitation for the stated scientific use cases.

Internal inconsistency that bears on the central 'calibration' claim: the black-hole appendix states they select a guidance scale γ = 0.003 for their own method, whereas Table 4 and the framing state CBG samples the true posterior at γ = 1 with no guidance scale. Using a tuned tempered likelihood on the flagship scientific task directly contradicts the calibrated-inference claim and needs clarification.

Consistency is only asymptotic in K; finite-sample behavior (weight degeneracy for sharp likelihoods in high dimensions) is not analyzed. The claim in Section 5.3 that the gradient-free estimator has lower variance 'in general' is contradicted by their own Appendix C/Figure 5, which shows the gradient-based method is better in a large region (t ≲ 0.3).

The black-hole evaluation uses only PSNR, a reconstruction metric, not a distributional/calibration metric. Since the paper's core thesis is calibrated posterior sampling, evaluating on PSNR does not actually test the central claim; a posterior-coverage or calibration metric would be needed.

Presentation issues: the proof of Theorem 4.2 contains a garbled line ('p(x)·q(x)=p(x′)p(x′)...'), and the practical relevance of Theorem 4.3 to the authors' own framework (they note one needs a tempered conditional model to extract tempered gradients) is left unresolved relative to their γ-tuning practice.

strengths: The paper gives a crisp, formal characterization of why common diffused-likelihood approximations are biased: Theorem 4.1 (posterior-mean/DPS), Theorem 4.2 (Gaussian/ΠGDM-style approximation), and Theorem 4.3 (guidance-scale exponentiation). Theorem 4.3 in particular is a clean, correct observation (via Jensen) that p(y|x_t,γ) ≠ p(y|x_t)^γ, which formalizes a genuinely under-discussed issue.

The gradient-free estimator (Equation 20) is simple and elegant: a self-normalized importance-weighting of (a_t x^(i) - x_t)/b_t^2 with weights w_i = p(y|x^(i)). It is consistent as K→∞, avoids differentiating through the sampler, and supports non-differentiable rewards, which is a practically useful property.

The Bayesian inference benchmark (Section 6.1) is reasonably executed: Figure 3 shows CBG improving toward the optimal C2ST of 0.5 as compute increases while baselines plateau, and Table 1 reports a comprehensive set of likelihood-based and likelihood-free comparisons with standard deviations.
The paper honestly acknowledges the main limitation (the need to sample from p(x|x_t), i.e., computational cost) and points to few-step models as a possible remedy.
weaknesses: The most directly relevant prior work is missing: SMC/particle-based guidance methods (e.g., Twisted Diffusion Sampler, 'Practical and Asymptotically Exact Conditional Sampling in Diffusion Models', and related SMC guidance work). Equation 20 is essentially a single self-normalized importance-sampling step, which is a degenerate case of these methods; SMC approaches already provide consistent posterior sampling and, crucially, address the weight-degeneracy problem via resampling/twisting. Not positioning or comparing against them substantially weakens the novelty claim.

The central 'calibration' thesis is not validated in the high-dimensional experiment. Black-hole imaging is evaluated only with PSNR, a point-estimate reconstruction metric that says nothing about posterior calibration. The experiment used to claim scalability to scientific tasks does not measure the property the paper is about.

There is an internal contradiction about guidance scale. Appendix F states 'CBG does not tune a guidance scale since we aim to sample from the true distribution p(x|y) at γ = 1,' yet Appendix G reports selecting γ = 0.003 for CBG on black-hole imaging. If a tempered likelihood is used, the black-hole results do not sample the true Bayesian posterior, undermining the 'calibrated' claim for the flagship scientific application.

The gradient-based estimator is much worse than the gradient-free one (avg C2ST 0.681 vs 0.527 in Table 1; Task 5 at 0.852), so the paper's contribution effectively reduces to a single estimator. The variance argument in Section 5.3 is informal and only weakly supported by Appendix C ('noticeably not by much'), so the claimed superiority of the gradient-free estimator is not firmly established.

Weight degeneracy is the elephant in the room. Using p(x|x_t) as the proposal with sharp likelihoods collapses the effective sample size, which is why K=512 and ~2h40 per image on an H100 are needed. The paper acknowledges this informally but offers no mitigation; the standard fix (SMC resampling/twisting/rejuvenation) is not considered, which limits the method's practical value.

The empirical evidence for the main claims is on low-dimensional toy problems (2–10D) with closed-form diffusion posteriors, precisely the regime where importance sampling is expected to succeed. This provides little evidence about scalability, and the margin over the best likelihood-free baseline (SNPE at 0.545 vs CBG at 0.527) is small.

On black-hole imaging, the reported PSNR for CBG (26.10, σ=3.83) is within noise of PnP-DM (26.07, σ=3.70) and DPS (25.86, σ=3.90), so 'match state-of-the-art' is essentially a tie, and it is achieved at a much higher computational cost. The marginal improvement does not obviously justify the cost.

The theory, while correct in spirit, largely formalizes what is already empirically known (that DPS/ΠGDM-style approximations are not exact posterior samplers). The proofs are somewhat technical/hand-wavy in places (e.g., the O(σ_t^3) expansion in Theorem 4.1 that concludes an exact affine/constant result; garbled lines in the Theorem 4.2 proof), and the paper overstates the framing that existing work merely 'maximizes reward' rather than aiming for posterior sampling.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: the paper correctly identifies that common test-time guidance methods (DPS/ΠGDM/NDTM) do not sample from the true Bayesian posterior, and formalizes this with Theorems 4.1–4.3, which characterize the structural bias of the posterior-mean approximation, the Gaussian posterior approximation, and guidance-scale exponentiation.

The proposed consistent estimators are technically sound: the gradient-based reparameterization estimator (Eq. 16) and the gradient-free REINFORCE estimator (Eq. 20) are correct self-normalized importance-weighted estimators, and the derivation showing the gradient-free form reduces to a Tweedie posterior-mean estimate (Eq. 21) is elegant and insightful.

Strong and controlled empirical evidence on the SBI benchmark (Section 6.1): CBG (gradient-free) achieves near-optimal C2ST (0.527 average) and clearly beats all diffusion baselines and most likelihood-free methods, and Figure 3 demonstrates the crucial property that performance improves monotonically with compute, directly supporting the consistency claim.

Demonstrates scaling to a high-dimensional scientific inverse problem (black hole imaging), matching SOTA PSNR (26.10 vs 25.86 DPS / 26.07 PnP-DM) without requiring likelihood gradients, and the qualitative reconstructions in Figures 6–7 are competitive.

Good reproducibility practices: detailed hyperparameter sweeps (Tables 3–4), task definitions (Appendix E), and experimental protocol details (Appendix G), plus an honest limitations discussion acknowledging the sampling cost.
weaknesses: The paper's central claim is about calibrated (distributional) posterior sampling, but this is only directly measured (C2ST) in low-dimensional tasks with closed-form priors/posteriors. The high-dimensional black-hole experiment reports only PSNR, a point-estimate metric, so the end-to-end calibration benefit is never demonstrated at scale—arguably the most important empirical test given the paper's thesis.

The low-dimensional experiments use closed-form diffusion posteriors p(x|x_t), bypassing the diffusion model's approximation error; thus they isolate the estimator but do not validate the full pipeline. The high-dim experiment uses a learned prior but does not measure calibration, leaving a gap between the theoretical consistency guarantee and demonstrated practical calibration.

Computational cost is very high: ~2h40 per image on a single H100 with K=512, M=50, and O(NM) per sample. The consistency claim requires large K, so the practical regime where the estimator is reliable may be prohibitively expensive; the limitation section acknowledges this but offers only speculative few-step remedies.

Consistency of the self-normalized estimators implicitly assumes well-behaved importance weights. For sharp likelihoods—exactly the regime the method targets—the weights can be degenerate/heavy-tailed, and finite-K bias can be severe. The paper discusses this qualitatively (Section 5.3) but provides no rigorous variance/convergence bound or diagnostic.

Moderate novelty: the estimators are natural applications of reparameterization, REINFORCE, and self-normalized importance sampling. The primary novel contribution is the diagnosis of bias and the self-normalized formulation rather than fundamentally new methodology.

Some proof rigor concerns: Theorem 4.1's argument (setting p(y|x_t)=p(y|x̂) implies tr(Σ_t ∇²p)=0, hence ∇²p=0) is heuristic—a single trace equation does not in general imply a zero Hessian—and the proof invokes t≪1 while the theorem is stated for all 0<t<1. Theorem 4.3/4.1 rely on a 'constant likelihood' trivial-case exclusion that weakens the 'regardless of the task' framing in the abstract.

On the high-dimensional task the method essentially matches rather than clearly outperforms baselines, so it is not conclusively shown that the calibration improvement translates into meaningfully better scientific reconstructions or uncertainty quantification.

strengths: Identifies and formalizes an important issue: common test-time guidance approximations (posterior mean, Gaussian posterior, optimal control) are inconsistent estimators of the diffused likelihood, with counterexamples in Theorem 4.1 and Example 4.2.
Shows that naive guidance-scale rescaling for tempered posteriors is incorrect, with a clean proof (Theorem 4.3), clarifying a common misconception in classifier-free guidance and diffusion guidance.

Proposes a consistent gradient-free estimator (Eq. 20) via REINFORCE/self-normalized importance sampling that does not require differentiable rewards or likelihood gradients, enabling calibrated posterior sampling in principle.

On the SBI benchmark, CBG improves C2ST with more compute and achieves the best average C2ST among compared methods, with bias-variance analysis in the appendix supporting consistency in the low-dimensional analytic setting.
Provides a renoising trick to use one-step models, making the method feasible with pretrained models, and demonstrates it on black hole imaging and image inverse problems.
Includes an honest limitations section about the measure-zero likelihood manifold issue and discusses when over-optimizing methods may outperform calibrated sampling on task metrics.
weaknesses: The consistency guarantee of the proposed estimators relies on exact samples from p(x|x_t); in practice, DDPM inner loops are truncated and the renoising trick is heuristic, so the full sampling procedure is not guaranteed to be consistent. The paper does not theoretically justify the renoising approximation or bound its bias.

The flagship black hole experiment uses a guidance scale γ=0.003 (Appendix H), which corresponds to a heavily tempered posterior and contradicts the paper's central claim of calibrated sampling. No calibration metrics (e.g., coverage, C2ST) are reported for the black hole or image tasks; only task metrics (PSNR) are shown.

Computational cost is extreme: the SOTA PSNR on black hole requires ~6 hours per sample (K=65536) versus ~24 seconds for DPS; at comparable wall-clock (renoise K=512, 2.9 min), the gain over DPS is marginal (26.10 vs 25.86 PSNR). This limits practical significance.

The paper criticizes guidance-scale rescaling (Eq. 12) but then uses a guidance scale in the black hole and prompt alignment experiments; it does not clarify whether this scale is applied correctly (inside the expectation) or whether it still yields calibrated samples.
Missing comparison to relevant posterior sampling methods such as DCPS (cited in related work) and SMC-based diffusion posterior samplers, which also aim at calibrated inference.

Image-domain experiments (super-resolution, prompt alignment) are mostly qualitative; Table 5 shows CBG leads PSNR but trails strong baselines on LPIPS/FID, and the comparison uses a different prior model and number of steps, limiting conclusions.

Reproducibility concerns: the code URL is incomplete; the black hole mean-flow model is trained on synthetic data generated from the diffusion model (not public); huge compute requirements hinder reproducibility of the main PSNR result.

The theoretical results are somewhat expected to experts (DPS bias is known), and the proposed estimator is essentially self-normalized importance sampling, so originality is moderate; concurrent work (Potaptchik et al., 2026) trains few-step models for the same estimators.

strengths: Correctly diagnoses that the widely used posterior-mean (DPS, Eq. 7) and Gaussian (PiGDM, Eq. 8) approximations are inconsistent estimators of the diffused likelihood, and gives some formal backing (Thm 4.1, Example 4.2). The identification of the failure mode is coherent and the accompanying figures (Fig. 1, 2) communicate it clearly.

The tempering analysis (Eq. 12 vs. Eq. 13, Thm 4.3) correctly notes that rescaling the diffused-likelihood gradient is not equivalent to tempering the likelihood inside the integral; this is a useful clarification (though closely related to the prior observation of Sun et al. 2024, which the authors cite).

The gradient-free estimator (Eq. 20) is a valid, self-normalized importance-weighting/Tweedie estimator, and the derivation (Eqs. 17-19) is essentially correct. It is simple to implement and does not require differentiating through the likelihood or the sampler.

The simulation-based-inference benchmark (Fig. 3, Table 1) provides a reasonable empirical demonstration that the estimator approaches the true posterior as K grows (C2ST -> 0.5), whereas most baselines plateau.
The renoising trick (Eq. 21) is a practical way to use one-step/few-step models, and the paper is honest about it being heuristic. The Limitations section (measure-zero likelihood overlap) is candid.
Code is released and the experimental setup is described in detail in the appendix.
weaknesses: A major, decisive related-work omission: sequential Monte Carlo / particle-based guidance methods (Twisted Diffusion Sampler, Wu et al. 2023; Monte Carlo Guided Diffusion, Cardoso et al. 2024; Particle Denoising Diffusion Sampler, Phillips et al. 2024) solve exactly the 'calibrated posterior sampling with a diffusion prior' problem using the same likelihood-weighted particle/score mechanism as the gradient-free CBG estimator (Eq. 20/22). None of these are cited or compared. This substantially undercuts the claim of a 'novel consistent framework' and the paper's originality.

The theoretical results are weak existence statements: they only show that there EXISTS some x_t at which the approximation fails, without quantifying the bias magnitude or demonstrating that it distorts the sampled distribution. Almost any approximation fails somewhere, so this does not support the strong claim that existing methods 'usually do not converge to the true posterior even with more compute.'

The headline claim of a 'new state-of-the-art PSNR in black hole image reconstruction' is not compute-matched. At K=512 CBG reaches 26.10 dB vs. PnP-DM 26.07 dB (essentially a tie), and it only exceeds baselines at K=65536 (27.08 dB) at ~6 hours/sample versus 45 s for PnP-DM -- a >200x compute increase. The abstract states the SOTA claim without this caveat.

No unguided/prior-only baseline is reported for black-hole imaging, so it is unclear how much of the PSNR is attributable to guidance versus the prior. The reported guidance scale gamma=0.003 (essentially negligible guidance) is a red flag that the likelihood may be doing very little work.

The comparison to likelihood-free SBI methods (NLE/NPE/SNLE/...) is not like-for-like: CBG uses the exact likelihood p(y|x), whereas those methods only use samples y|x. Claiming to 'outperform' them is an unfair framing.

Table 1 does not support 'the best distributional fit for every task by far': on Task 3 the gradient-free CBG (0.584) is worse than SNLE (0.578), and several reported gaps (e.g., 0.505 vs 0.506) are within reported standard deviations; no significance testing is provided.

The super-resolution experiment (Table 5) uses a different prior model (pMF) and a different number of diffusion steps than the baselines -- acknowledged in the appendix -- so the numbers are not directly comparable, and CBG trails badly on LPIPS and FID. The quantitative claim of 'effectiveness' is therefore weak.

Practical usefulness is limited by compute: the gradient-based estimator is acknowledged to be inferior, and the recommended gradient-free estimator needs K up to 65,536 samples per step, plus an extra mean-flow model trained on synthetic samples generated by the diffusion model, which conflicts with the 'training-free' positioning. The renoising construction is heuristic with no theoretical justification.

The paper frames its contribution against 'reward maximization' methods, but the distinction between guidance-as-reward-maximization and guidance-as-posterior-sampling is well known, so this framing overstates the novelty of the diagnosis.

Reproducibility issues: the code link is truncated, and the black-hole evaluation trains on synthetic samples from the pretrained model rather than the true data, which is not validated against real data.

strengths: Provides a clean theoretical account of why common test-time guidance estimators are inconsistent: Theorem 4.1 (posterior-mean), Example 4.2 (Gaussian posterior), and Theorem 4.3 (guidance-scale/tempering) formalize known failure modes with reasonable proofs in the appendix.

The proposed CBG framework is principled: both the reparameterization estimator (Eq. 16) and the REINFORCE-style gradient-free estimator (Eq. 20) are consistent importance-weighted estimators of the diffused likelihood/posterior score in the idealized setting where exact samples from p(x|x_t) are available. The gradient-free version is particularly attractive since it needs no gradients through the sampler or likelihood.

The empirical study is broad and multi-domain: an analytic Bayesian-inference benchmark (C2ST), black-hole imaging (PSNR/chi^2), super-resolution, and prompt alignment, with clear scaling behavior. Figure 3 and Appendix Figure 8 show that only CBG drives bias toward zero as K grows, while baselines plateau at biased solutions.
Reproducibility is good: detailed hyperparameter sweeps (Tables 3-4), full task specifications (Appendix F), training details for the mean-flow model (Appendix H), and code release promised.
The limitations section is honest about the measure-zero-overlap failure mode and the fact that reward-maximizing methods can beat the calibrated sampler on task metrics.

Demonstrating a consistent, compute-scalable guidance mechanism has genuine value for scientific inference where uncertainty calibration matters, and the tiled gradient-free variant for SR is a useful practical contribution.
weaknesses: The manuscript overclaims: the text states the gradient-free method achieves 'the best distributional fit for every task by far,' but Table 1 shows Langevin+REINFORCE is better on Task 1 (0.502 vs 0.505) and MCMC-NUTS is better on Task 2 (0.511 vs 0.513). The reported average gains over strong baselines (SNPE 0.545, NUTS 0.553) are modest and within/near reported standard deviations, so statistical significance is unclear.

One of the two central contributions, the gradient-based estimator, is empirically weak (average C2ST 0.681), underperforming DPS, LGD, SCG, and several likelihood-free methods. This substantially weakens the 'consistent framework' narrative since only the gradient-free variant works in practice.

The headline 'state-of-the-art PSNR' on black-hole imaging (27.08) is obtained at K=65536 (~6 hours per sample) and, critically, with guidance scale gamma=0.003 rather than gamma=1. Sampling from a heavily tempered distribution is not sampling the calibrated Bayesian posterior, which is in tension with the paper's central thesis; at comparable compute (renoise K=512, 48s) CBG (25.36) is below PnP-DM (26.07).

Consistency is only guaranteed when x^(i) are exact samples from p(x|x_t). The practical estimator relies on the heuristic renoise trick (Eq. 21) with a deterministic one-step model, so the practical procedure is not provably consistent and the theoretical guarantee does not transfer to the experiments as run.

The Bayesian-inference benchmark uses analytic priors with exact closed-form diffusion posteriors, an idealized setting that does not test the regime where p(x|x_t) must be approximated by a pretrained model, which is the actual setting of interest for the proposed framework.

Related work on asymptotically exact particle/SMC/twisted diffusion posterior sampling (e.g., Twisted Diffusion Sampler / Twist, Monte Carlo guided diffusion, twisted SMC) is not discussed, even though these methods pursue the same goal of consistent posterior sampling via likelihood-weighted particles. This omission weakens the novelty claim for the 'consistent framework' and should be addressed.

Presentation issues: Figure 3's caption/axis semantics are confusing, and the abstract/conclusion's framing of 'significantly outperform' is not supported by the magnitude of the reported improvements.
